If a new word is substituted into the place of an old word, over time the new word will adopt, in a general way, the meaning of the old word. But it takes some time. In the short term, if words are prohibited or eliminated, people will have difficulty expressing their concepts. And the new word will never mean exactly the same thing as the old word.

For example, the word "retarded" was prohibited and replaced by "mentally handicapped," and that in turn was replaced by "special needs." All three mean slightly different things. The two euphemisms are softer in their impact, and the words have different connotations. Retarded suggests slow; mentally handicapped suggests someone who has been slowed; speical needs suggests we should be helping someone who has been slowed. Another example, "crippled" was replaced by "handicapped." Crippled implies an inherent disability, but handicapped suggests a person is somehow held back or restrained.
